flawed_step: Line 0052 (the concluding step of Lemma 1's proof, lines 0048-0053): from n/2 + alpha*n <= n - 1, i.e. alpha <= 1/2 - 1/n, the proof asserts a contradiction 'for any fixed alpha > 0 and sufficiently large n'. This is backwards: for fixed alpha in (0, 1/2) the inequality alpha <= 1/2 - 1/n is SATISFIED for all large n, so no contradiction arises and Lemma 1 (delta(G) > alpha*n) is not established. The lemma is in fact false, and every later step (0061-0065) depends on it.
counterexample:
A. The inequality derived at line 0051 is not contradictory. Take alpha = 0.1 and n = 100. Line 0051 yields alpha <= 1/2 - 1/n = 0.49. Since 0.1 <= 0.49, the supposed contradiction at line 0052 does not occur; larger n only weakens the constraint (limit 0.5), so 'sufficiently large n' makes the situation better, not worse, for any fixed alpha < 1/2.

B. Explicit graph showing Lemma 1 itself is false (so the gap is not patchable). Let n = 10, alpha = 0.1, V = {1,...,10}. Let vertices 1..9 form a complete graph K_9, and let vertex 10 be isolated (no edges at all).
  - Expansion hypothesis holds with alpha = 0.1: the required bound is |N(S)| >= n/2 + alpha*n = 5 + 1 = 6 for every S with |S| = n/2 = 5. Any such S contains at least 4 vertices of {1,...,9}. For u in {1,...,9}, N(u) = {1,...,9} \ {u}; the union of two or more such sets is all of {1,...,9}. Hence N(S) = {1,...,9} (vertex 10 contributes nothing, and 10 is in no N(u)), so |N(S)| = 9 >= 6. This holds for every one of the C(10,5) = 252 sets S, so the hypothesis is satisfied.
  - Conclusion of Lemma 1 fails: delta(G) = deg(10) = 0, which is NOT > alpha*n = 1.

C. Trace of the proof's own construction on this instance, showing exactly where it breaks. Take v = 10, deg(v) = 0 <= alpha*n = 1, as in line 0022. Then N[v] = {10}, U = V \ N[v] = {1,...,9}, |U| = 9 > n/2 - 1 = 4 (lines 0026-0030 check out). Choose T = {1,2,3,4} subset of U with |T| = n/2 - 1 = 4, and S = {10,1,2,3,4}, so |S| = 5 = n/2 (lines 0031-0032 check out). Then N(S) = N(10) union N(T) = empty union {1,...,9} = {1,...,9}, and indeed |N(S)| = 9 <= n - 1 = 9, so the bound at line 0047 is correct and tight. But the expansion requirement is only |N(S)| >= 6, and 9 >= 6 holds. So line 0048's inequality n/2 + alpha*n <= n - 1 reads 6 <= 9: true, no contradiction. Line 0051 gives 0.1 <= 0.5 - 0.1 = 0.4: true. Line 0052's claimed contradiction is therefore simply false on this instance.

D. Downstream consequence: line 0062 uses |N(v_i)| > alpha*n to conclude N(v_i) intersect W_{i+1} is nonempty. In the graph above with alpha = 0.1, take k = 2 and W_1 = W_2 = {1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,10} (|W_i| = 9 >= (1-alpha)n = 9). Line 0055 permits 'choose any v_1 in W_1', e.g. v_1 = 10; then N(v_1) = empty and N(v_1) intersect W_2 = empty, so the inductive step of lines 0058-0064 cannot proceed. (The theorem's statement can still be rescued here by picking v_1 in {1,...,8}, so this is a genuine gap in the proof rather than a counterexample to the theorem.)
reasoning_summary: Verified step by step. Lines 0010-0018 restate the hypotheses and announce Lemma 1 (delta(G) > alpha*n). Lines 0019-0021 argue alpha < 1/2; this sub-argument is already slightly defective, since alpha = 1/2 gives |N(S)| >= n, which is not impossible (K_n achieves |N(S)| = n), so only alpha <= 1/2 follows -- a minor, non-fatal boundary slip. Lines 0022-0032 (contradiction hypothesis deg(v) <= alpha*n, U = V \ N[v], |U| >= (1-alpha)n - 1 > n/2 - 1, choice of T and S = {v} union T with |S| = n/2) are correct. Lines 0033-0047 are also correct: V is the disjoint union of {v}, N(v), U, so N(u) subset of N(v) union U for u in T, hence N(S) subset of N(v) union U and |N(S)| <= deg(v) + (n - deg(v) - 1) = n - 1. Line 0051's rearrangement (alpha <= 1/2 - 1/n) is correct algebra. The failure is at line 0052: alpha <= 1/2 - 1/n is exactly what one expects for any fixed alpha < 1/2 and large n, so it is not a contradiction; the derived bound |N(S)| <= n - 1 is far too weak to conflict with the expansion bound n/2 + alpha*n. The lemma is not merely unproved but false: K_9 plus an isolated tenth vertex satisfies the expansion hypothesis with alpha = 0.1 yet has minimum degree 0. Since the path construction (lines 0061-0064) rests entirely on |N(v_i)| > alpha*n, and line 0055 allows an arbitrary choice of v_1, the whole argument collapses at this point. Stopping at line 0052 with the witness above.
